title: ClockRail re-renders every second even when showSeconds is off
author: claude[bot]
body:
**What to optimise**

The two-zone clock rail at the top of the home screen (`ClockRail`) is wrapped in `React.memo` with a custom comparator whose whole job is to stop it re-rendering more often than the visible text actually changes. But the comparator always buckets time by *second*, even when the user has turned seconds off in Settings. With seconds hidden, the rail only needs to visually update once a minute (`HH:MM`), yet it still tears down and reformats both zone cards 60 times for every one of those updates — pure wasted work on the app's one truly continuous hot loop, for a screen that's designed to sit on and be glanced at from across a room.

Fix: when `showSeconds` is false, bucket the memo comparison by minute instead of by second, so the component only re-renders when the visible `HH:MM` value can actually have changed.

**Where**

`app/components/ClockRail.tsx:223-235` — the `ClockRail` memo comparator:

```
export const ClockRail = memo(ClockRailImpl, (prev, next) => {
  if (Math.floor(prev.now.getTime() / 1000) !== Math.floor(next.now.getTime() / 1000)) {
    return false;
  }
  ...
```

This always uses a 1000ms bucket regardless of `next.showSeconds`, even though `showSeconds` is already one of the props this same comparator checks for equality a few lines down (`prev.showSeconds === next.showSeconds`).

**Expected gain**

`useNow` ticks at a strict 1Hz for as long as the app is open (`app/lib/useNow.ts`), and `ClockRail` sits directly under `HomeScreen`'s per-tick `now` state, so today it re-renders, and each `ZoneCard` re-runs `formatInZone` + `zoneAbbr`, 3,600 times an hour regardless of the `showSeconds` setting. With seconds hidden, only 60 of those renders per hour (the minute rollovers) actually change what's on screen — the other ~98% are pure waste. Bucketing by minute when `showSeconds` is false cuts this component's render/format rate by roughly 60x for as long as that setting is off. I arrived at this by reading the comparator logic against `useNow`'s tick alignment and confirming `showSeconds` is a real, user-facing Settings toggle (`app/app/index.tsx:371`, wired through `SettingsModal`), not a hypothetical.

**Which CLAUDE.md priority this serves**

Battery / "the application MUST stay minimal, fast" for the always-on 1-second render loop, on the exact screen CLAUDE.md calls the core use case ("monitoring multiple timezones... from a distance"). It's the same class of hot-loop waste CLAUDE.md calls out directly ("the 1-second ticker... run constantly on modest hardware, so... an avoidable re-render there costs real battery and real smoothness").

**Scope check (STEP 4)**

- One file (`app/components/ClockRail.tsx`), one function (the memo comparator), roughly 5-8 changed lines.
- No architecture change, no state moved, no new files, no new refs.
- Does not touch any CLAUDE.md invariant: no beep pool, no `BEEP_LEAD_MS`, no Notifee/native code, no passed-cue derivation, no backend/account/sync surface.
- Correctness preserved: when `showSeconds` is true the bucket stays 1000ms (identical behaviour to today); when false, the visible `HH:MM` text is provably unchanged for every skipped render, so nothing the user sees regresses. The existing `prev.showSeconds === next.showSeconds` check already forces an immediate re-render the instant the setting is toggled, so switching modes stays responsive.

**How to verify**

On the Xiaomi Mi A2 Lite, turn off "Show seconds" in Settings, leave the home screen open, and attach a JS profiler (Flipper / Chrome remote debugger) or a temporary render counter to `ClockRailImpl`. Before the fix: expect ~1 render/sec (3,600/hour). After: expect ~1 render/min (60/hour), with the displayed `HH:MM` staying pixel-identical throughout and still ticking over correctly at each minute boundary. Also confirm toggling "Show seconds" back on immediately restores per-second updates with no stale digits.

title: Simplify alertKeyExtractor in CueEditModal.tsx to use String directly
author: yanukadeneth99
body:
What's worth improving
In app/components/CueEditModal.tsx there's a small arrow function that only wraps String() around its argument and returns the result. Since String itself already has exactly that signature (take one value, return its string form), the wrapper function is unnecessary indirection - it adds a line of code and a name to read without doing anything String doesn't already do on its own.

Where
app/components/CueEditModal.tsx:30

Current code:
const alertKeyExtractor = (item: number) => String(item);

Sonar rule and message
Rule typescript:S7770. Sonar's exact message: "arrow function 'alertKeyExtractor' is equivalent to `String`. Use `String` directly."

Suggested fix
Replace the wrapper with a direct reference to the built-in function:
const alertKeyExtractor = String;

Why this is safe
alertKeyExtractor is passed to a FlatList as its keyExtractor prop (comment above it explains it's hoisted so the list gets a stable reference across renders). FlatList calls keyExtractor(item, index) - String(item, index) still just converts item to a string and ignores the extra index argument, exactly like the current (item) => String(item) does. There is no behavior change, no change to what key strings are produced, and no interaction with the alert/alarm scheduling logic elsewhere in this file - this is purely the render key for the alert-minutes option list.

Smallest safe change
A one-line edit: swap the arrow-function body for the bare String reference, keeping the same variable name, the same hoisted-outside-the-component placement (so the existing comment about a stable reference for FlatList still applies), and the same export/visibility.

CLAUDE.md invariants to keep in mind
This file is part of the Alert System's CueEditModal, so any touch here should stay narrowly scoped to this one line - do not touch the scheduling logic (`rescheduling` must keep flowing through `rescheduleInBackground` per CLAUDE.md) or any of the alert-minutes list rendering/behavior around it. body:
**CI fix applied.** The ESLint bump to 10.9.1 broke `npm run lint` with:

```
TypeError: Error while loading rule 'react/display-name': contextOrFilename.getFilename is not a function
```

**Root cause:** ESLint 10 removed the deprecated `context.getFilename()` API. `eslint-config-next`'s bundled `eslint-plugin-react` (7.37.5, the latest release) still calls it whenever `settings.react.version` is `"detect"` — which is the default `eslint-config-next` sets. There's no newer `eslint-plugin-react`/`eslint-config-next` release yet that avoids this call, so bumping either wouldn't help.

**Fix:** added an override in `website/eslint.config.mjs` pinning `settings.react.version` to the installed React version (`19.2.8`), which skips the `"detect"` codepath entirely (and the crashing call) without touching any dependency versions.

Verified `npm run lint` and `npm run build` both pass locally in `website/`.

**Worth checking:** when `eslint-plugin-react` ships a fix for ESLint 10's context API, this pin can likely be removed — worth a follow-up note or dependabot will just keep bumping React versions here if `react` itself is upgraded (this pin would then need to track it, or switch to `"detect"` once upstream is fixed).

title: fix: enforce native-only final-3s beep on web
author: claude[bot]
body:
Closes #187.

## What changed and why

The "Final 3s beep" (3-2-1 ticks + a "go" tone at zero for the primary cue) is documented as a **native-only** feature, but two `useEffect`s that drive it — the audio pre-warm/prime effect and the beep scheduling effect — had no `Platform` guard. On the web build, once any user gesture unlocked the browser's audio autoplay policy, the timer-driven `play()` calls fired, producing an unexpected beep in the final 3 seconds of a cue. Worse, the Settings toggle that would silence it is intentionally hidden on web, so there was **no way to turn it off**.

The fix adds an early `if (Platform.OS === "web") return;` to the top of both effects, matching the existing web-guard idiom already used throughout `app/app/index.tsx`. This makes the implementation match the documented invariant with a minimal, low-risk change.

### Watch out for

- The change is intentionally minimal: only the two effect bodies are gated. The `useAudioPlayer` hook calls stay unconditional (Rules of Hooks), so an unused player is created on web but never primed or played — harmless.
- All native beep machinery is untouched: the 2-player pool alternation, `BEEP_LEAD_MS` predictive scheduling, `SETTLE_MS` pre-warm, `goFiredForRef` one-shot gating, and `pendingBeepTimersRef` cleanup all remain reachable on native.
- The SettingsModal toggle stays hidden on web (correct — the feature can't fire there now).
- I did not add the optional `setFinalBeep(false)` on web: with both effects bailing out the flag is inert on web, so forcing it would be dead state churn.
- `npx expo-doctor` reports pre-existing dependency version drift (11 packages) unrelated to this change — no dependencies were touched.

The app has a "Final 3s beep" that plays short beeps for the last 3 seconds (3-2-1) and a "go" tone at zero for the soonest cue. This is documented as a **native-only** feature (Android/iOS). On the **web build**, two problems combine:

1. The code that produces the beep is not limited to native — it runs on web too.
2. The Settings toggle that would let a user turn the beep off is deliberately hidden on web.

The net effect: a web user hears a beep in the final 3 seconds of a cue that they were never meant to hear, and there is **no switch anywhere in the app to turn it off**.

## Where it is

- `app/app/index.tsx:385` — `const [finalBeep, setFinalBeep] = useState(true);` (default ON, never forced off on web).
- `app/app/index.tsx:503` — the beep "pre-warm/prime" effect. No `Platform.OS` guard, so it runs on web.
- `app/app/index.tsx:565`-`686` — the beep scheduling effect. No `Platform.OS` guard; it calls `beepPlayerA/B.play()` / `goPlayer.play()` on web (see `scheduleBeep` around `app/app/index.tsx:637`-`649`).
- `app/app/index.tsx:962` — load path only turns the beep off if storage explicitly holds `"false"`; a fresh web install leaves it `true`.
- `app/components/SettingsModal.tsx:128`-`142` — the "Final 3s beep" row is wrapped in `{!isWeb ? (...) : null}`, so the toggle is **hidden on web**. The comment there states the intent plainly: *"Native-only: web's autoplay policies block short SFX ... Hidden on web to avoid a setting that lies."*

## How it happens (step by step)

1. A user opens the web app (`web.output: "static"` build). `finalBeep` initialises to `true` and there is no web override.
2. The user interacts with the page normally — adds/edits a cue, taps around. Any user gesture unlocks the browser's audio autoplay policy for the document, so later `HTMLMediaElement.play()` calls from timers are allowed.
3. A cue counts down. The scheduling effect (`app/app/index.tsx:565`) runs every tick on web too, detects `primaryTotal` at 4/3/2/1 and schedules `player.play()` via `setTimeout`.
4. Those `play()` calls now succeed (audio was unlocked in step 2), so the beep is audible in the final 3 seconds.
5. The user goes to Settings to silence it — but the "Final 3s beep" row is not rendered on web, so there is no way to turn it off. (Even the mid-countdown "toggle off" path in the effect at `app/app/index.tsx:566` can never be reached, because the toggle can't be flipped.)

## Who it affects and how badly

- **Platform:** web build only (the shipped web app).
- **Feature:** the final-3s beep on the primary cue.
- **Severity:** low — it does not crash (all `play()` calls are wrapped in try/catch at `app/app/index.tsx:623` and `:639`) and it does not affect alarms. For a "minimal, distraction-free" broadcast tool, an unexpected and unsilenceable sound is exactly the kind of surprise the product is meant to avoid.
- **Frequency:** every primary cue that reaches its final 3 seconds while the web tab is open and has had any prior user interaction.

title: perf(app): stop PassedStrip re-rendering every second (#210)
author: claude[bot]
body:
Closes #210.

## What changed

`PassedStrip` was exported with a plain `memo(PassedStripImpl)` — no comparator. Because `HomeScreen` re-renders every second (the 1Hz ticker) and passes a fresh `now` Date plus new inline `onTap`/`onRequestDelete` closures each tick, the default shallow compare saw "props differ" every second and re-rendered the strip in full — even though its visible `ago` text only changes once a minute after the first 60s. A passed cue can stay on screen for hours (until zone1 midnight), so this was steady waste on the app's one always-on hot loop.

This adds a bucketed `memo` comparator that re-renders only when the visible text can actually change:

- The `ago` label (per-second under 60s, per-minute after) — computed via a shared `agoLabelFor` helper so the component and comparator can't drift.
- `block` (by reference, same as `QueuedRow`) and `is24Hour`.
- `onTap`/`onRequestDelete` are deliberately **not** compared: they are new closures every tick but always close over the same `block.id`, so a skipped render keeps a correctly-bound handler.

Matches the existing `ClockRail`/`QueuedRow`/`PrimaryCard` optimisation pattern. One file, presentational only — no change to the stateless `passedAt` derivation, alarms, beep pool, or native/CI config.

## Watch out for

- **Gating on the label, not raw `now`**: unlike the sibling comparators (which bucket `Math.floor(now/1000)`), this one gates on the actual `agoLabelFor` string. That's intentional — bucketing on raw seconds would still re-render every second and defeat the fix. Worth confirming the 59s→1m transition still lands on the right tick.
- **Excluding the callbacks from the comparator** is what actually delivers the reduction; if they were included (mirroring the literal sibling code) the closures would force a re-render every tick. Safe because they only capture `block.id`, which is stable for the strip's lifetime — but verify tap/× still work after a long idle.
- `expo-doctor`: 20/20 checks pass.

title: perf(app): bucket QueuedRow re-renders to its visible label
author: claude[bot]
body:
Closes #222.

## What changed

`QueuedRow`'s `React.memo` comparator forced a re-render on every 1-second home tick by bucketing on the raw `Math.floor(now/1000)` value, and it also compared `prev.onTap === next.onTap` — but `onTap` is an inline arrow allocated fresh on every `HomeScreen` render. Together that meant a row reading "12m left" was torn down and rebuilt ~60 times per visible change, once per second, on the always-on ticker.

The fix mirrors the merged `PassedStrip` precedent (#210):

- Add a private `remainingLabelFor(now, block, zone1, zone2)` helper that computes the `humanRemaining` label, used by **both** `QueuedRowImpl` (for display) and the comparator, so the label logic can't drift.
- Rewrite the comparator to compare the actual `"X left"` label string instead of the second-bucket, and drop the `onTap` comparison (documented, same reasoning as `PassedStrip`).

Displayed text is byte-identical; only render frequency drops. Per-second "Xs left" jitter is preserved for free because `humanRemaining` already switches to seconds at total ≤ 60, and comparing the label strings handles that boundary without extra branches.

Verification: `npx expo-doctor` → 20/20 checks passed. No `app.json`/dependency changes.

### Watch out for
- The comparator now calls `computeCountdown` (which runs `Intl.DateTimeFormat.formatToParts`) every tick per queued row even when the row won't re-render. This is the same trade-off `PassedStrip` already makes and is far cheaper than the full `QueuedRowImpl` JSX render it avoids — but worth a sanity check if the queued list ever grows very large.
- Dropping the `onTap` equality relies on the closure always targeting the same cue (`openEditor(b.id)`), which holds at the current call site in `index.tsx`.

title: QueuedRow re-renders every second even though its "Xm left" label only changes once a minute
author: claude[bot]
body:
**What to optimise**

Every cue below the top "Up Next" card is drawn by `QueuedRow`. Its `React.memo` comparator is supposed to stop a row re-rendering more often than the text on screen actually changes, but right now it always buckets by *second* — so a row that reads "12m left" gets torn down and rebuilt 60 times for every one of those minute-granularity updates, on the app's one continuous per-second loop. This is the same class of waste already fixed for `ClockRail` (#199) and `PassedStrip` (#210), just on a component neither of those touched.

**Where**

`app/components/QueuedRow.tsx:97-110` — the `QueuedRow` memo comparator:

```
export const QueuedRow = memo(QueuedRowImpl, (prev, next) => {
  // Re-render when the displayed second-bucket changes (covers minutes too).
  if (Math.floor(prev.now.getTime() / 1000) !== Math.floor(next.now.getTime() / 1000)) {
    return false;
  }
  ...
```

The row's own text (`app/lib/time.ts:177-183`, `humanRemaining`) already only changes every second while `total <= 60`, and only every 60 seconds once `total > 60` (`"${mm}m left"` / `"${hh}h ${mm}m left"`). The comparator ignores that and always uses a 1-second bucket.

**Expected gain**

Any queued cue that is more than a minute out (the common case — only the single soonest cue is ever shown as the "Up Next" primary; everything else lands here) currently re-renders, and re-runs `computeCountdown`, `shortCity`, `fmtHM`, and the full JSX/style tree, 60 times for each visible label change. Switching the bucket to minutes when `total > 60` (falling back to the existing per-second bucket only while `total <= 60`) cuts re-renders for those rows by up to ~98%, and the saving multiplies by however many queued cues are on screen at once (unlike the single fixed `ClockRail`/`PassedStrip` cards). This is the same reasoning already accepted for #199 and #210, applied to the one remaining per-tick list row that still buckets too finely.

**CLAUDE.md priority served**

Battery/CPU efficiency and smoothness of the always-on 1-second ticker ("the 1-second ticker, the countdown recomputation... run constantly on modest hardware, so a wasted allocation or an avoidable re-render there costs real battery and real smoothness") — directly the hot render path called out in CLAUDE.md, and it scales with cue count.

**Scope check (STEP 4)**

- 1 file (`app/components/QueuedRow.tsx`), roughly 15-20 changed lines, entirely inside the existing memo comparator. `QueuedRowImpl` itself is untouched.
- No architecture change: no state moves, no new component/file, no props added.
- No invariant touched: doesn't affect the beep pool, Notifee/alarm scheduling, passed-cue derivation, ABIs, or packaging. Purely a render-skip heuristic, same shape as the already-shipped `ClockRail` (#199 pending) and `PassedStrip` (#210, merged) fixes.

**How to verify on the Xiaomi Mi A2 Lite**

Add 2-3 cues each more than a minute out so several `QueuedRow`s are visible, attach the React DevTools profiler (or a `console.count` temporarily), and compare render counts over 60 seconds before/after: today each row should show ~60 renders/minute; after the fix, rows with `total > 60` should show close to 1 render/minute, only jumping back to per-second once a row crosses under the 60-second mark. Confirm the visible "Xm left" / "Xs left" text itself is unaffected — this only changes *how often* React re-renders, not what it shows.

Bumps [mermaid](https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid) from 11.17.2 to 12.0.0.
Release notes

Sourced from mermaid's releases.

mermaid@12.0.0

Mermaid 12.0.0 ships ELK as the bundled default layout engine, a new redux-color / neo default appearance, and two new diagram types: UML use case diagrams.

This is a breaking release (ES2024, Safari 17.4+, Node 22.12+). Existing flowcharts, state and class diagrams will re-lay out and recolour; add layout: dagre, theme: default and look: classic to your config to keep the old look. Full changelog below.

Major Changes

  • #8213 33442fd Thanks @​aloisklink! - chore!: require ES2024, Safari 17.4+, Node.JS v22.12+

    Mermaid is now built to target Safari 17.4+ and ES2024. If you need to support older browsers, you may need to polyfill or transpile mermaid.

    Safari 17.4+ has been chosen as the floor, as unlike Firefox/Chrome, older iOS devices don't get major Safari updates.

    Node.JS v22.12+ is also declared as requirement in our package.json files, but as mermaid requires a browser, this is mainly so we can use dependencies that also declare a Node.JS v22.12+ requirement, without causing issues for users when running npm install.

  • #8155 810893c Thanks @​ashishjain0512! - feat!: ELK is now bundled with mermaid and is the default layout algorithm.

    ELK previously shipped as a separate @mermaid-js/layout-elk package that sites had to install and register. It is now part of mermaid itself and registered automatically, so layout: elk — and the elk.stress, elk.force, elk.mrtree, elk.sporeOverlap, elk.box and elk.rectpacking variants — work with no setup.

    This changes how existing diagrams look. Flowchart, state, class, entity-relationship, requirement, use-case diagrams that do not specify a layout are now laid out by ELK instead of dagre. To keep the previous layout, set dagre explicitly:

    ---
config:
  layout: dagre
---

    or globally, mermaid.initialize({ layout: 'dagre' }).

    Mindmap is unchanged: it keeps laying out with cose-bilkent unless a layout is explicitly requested (in the tiny build, which ships neither ELK nor cose-bilkent, it falls back to dagre).

    Other notes:

    • ELK is loaded as a separate chunk in the ESM builds, so it is only fetched when a diagram actually uses it. The single-file IIFE build (mermaid.min.js) inlines it and grows by roughly 500 kB gzipped.
    • The tiny build deliberately omits ELK to stay small, and falls back to dagre for diagrams that ask for an ELK layout. Its size is unchanged.
    • @mermaid-js/layout-elk is no longer needed on normal builds — existing mermaid.registerLayoutLoaders(elkLayouts) calls keep working and can be removed. It is still published, and remains the way to add ELK to the tiny build.

title: Reset All silently keeps the "Final-3s beep" and "Minimize passed cues" settings instead of restoring defaults
author: claude[bot]

## What is wrong (plain language)

The **Reset All** button in Settings shows the promise *"This will clear all timers and settings. Are you sure?"*. It does clear the timers and most settings, but **two settings are quietly left untouched**: the *Final-3s beep* toggle and the *Auto-minimize passed cues* toggle. If a user turned either of these off (or on) and then hits Reset All, that choice survives the reset — both in the current session and across an app restart, because the value is written straight back to storage. The user is told everything was reset, but it wasn't.

## Where it is

- `app/app/index.tsx:1522` — `doReset()`
- `app/app/index.tsx:1529` — the `multiRemove([...])` list removes 8 keys but omits `autoMinimizePassed` and `finalBeep`.
- `app/app/index.tsx:1539` — the state setters reset 8 values (`setZone1`, `setIs24Hour`, … `setKeepOn`) but never call `setAutoMinimizePassed(true)` or `setFinalBeep(true)`.
- `app/app/index.tsx:1077` — the persist effect then re-writes `autoMinimizePassed` and `finalBeep` to storage using their unchanged in-memory values, so the omission also defeats the `multiRemove` even if the key had been listed.
- Both settings are user-reachable toggles: `app/components/SettingsModal.tsx:135` (`finalBeep`) and `:146` (`autoMinimizePassed`). Their defaults are `true` (see `app/app/index.tsx:960`/`:962`).

## How it happens (step by step)

1. User opens Settings and turns **Final-3s beep** OFF (a real broadcast choice — e.g. a live mic is open and any beep is unacceptable).
2. Later the user taps **Reset All** and confirms the *"clear all timers and settings"* dialog.
3. `doReset()` runs: it cancels alarms, `multiRemove`s the 8 listed keys, and resets 8 pieces of state. `finalBeep` (and `autoMinimizePassed`) are in neither list.
4. The state change triggers the persist effect at `index.tsx:1077`, which writes `["finalBeep", String(finalBeep)]` = `"false"` back to `AsyncStorage`.
5. Result: the beep stays OFF after reset, and on the next cold launch `loadData` reads `"false"` and keeps it OFF. Same mechanism for `autoMinimizePassed`.

## Who it affects and how badly

- **All platforms** for `autoMinimizePassed`; **Android/native** for `finalBeep` (it is native-only).
- Severity is **low-to-moderate**: no crash and no lost cues, but "Reset All" does not do what its own copy promises. A user relying on Reset to return to a known-good default state (a plausible move for an operator handing a device to the next shift) is left with two stale settings — and for `finalBeep` that can mean the final-3s countdown beep is silently absent (or present) contrary to the fresh-install default.

- I read `doReset()` end to end (`index.tsx:1522-1552`): the `multiRemove` array and the setter block both cover exactly `zone1, zone2, targetBlocks, is24Hour, alertMode, showSeconds, soundAlerts, keepOn` — `autoMinimizePassed` and `finalBeep` appear in neither.
- I confirmed both are genuine persisted settings (`index.tsx:1086-1087` write them; `:960`/`:962` load them with default `true`) and are user-toggleable (`SettingsModal.tsx:139-151`).

This is an omission, not a deliberate preserve (unlike `analyticsEnabled`, which CLAUDE.md explicitly documents as preserved on reset).

Add `"autoMinimizePassed"` and `"finalBeep"` to the `multiRemove` list, and add `setAutoMinimizePassed(true)` and `setFinalBeep(true)` to the setter block in `doReset()` — matching each field's documented default.
